Now what's important to understand is that we don't know where Zorusa worked specifically but we suspect northern Iran. Why is this important? Because during the branching age, the main centers of wealth were Mesopotamia, Egypt, and the Levant. So this was more like a colony where there was a lot of mining going on.

So what's going on here is basically the most human suffering in the world. Imagine Congo where they're using child slaves to dig for rare earths. It's a margin empire where war is a very common thing; violence is very common.

People are being kidnapped and forced to work in mines to get tin for the branch age economy. Zorusa is about here, either northeast Iran or northwest Iran. As I mentioned, the global economy is around here; this is where most of the wealth is. These people are poor, enslaved, and extremely violent.

Zorusa comes and he's a poet-prophet. He's a priest and he's singing songs to help people better understand the world around them. He's trying to remind them of who they really are: they're parts of God. So he says, "Listen with your own ears, with a bright mind. Choose truth from false creed. Each person for his own self before the final judgment comes."

The idea is that in the individual, what matters is yourself and what you do; what your family or tribe does doesn't matter. When you die, you will face the masta, the final judgment, not your family but you yourself. So what you must do is choose asha, the truth. What is the truth? Being virtuous because you yourself are virtue.

Zoroastrian priests write in a language called Avasten and it's beautiful, but I'm not one and don't want to butcher the language. Asha is the best of all that is good; ash is happiness, which belongs to the one who follows the righteous path for the sake of the best righteousness. How do you know you're doing asha? Because you are happy.

The metaphor is imagine a world where fat people don't exercise and only watch TV. You decide to go and work out and become more fit. You feel happier about yourself, but the problem is that you lose all your friends because they fear the truth.

All right, so this is some trusted poetry called agathas that we know Jorah thus sang or didn't write at this point. The two primal spirits who reveal themselves in vision as twins are the better and the bad in thought and word and action. Between these two, the wise ones choose; the foolish ones do not.

We in our nature always divide into good and bad halves: the asha and the douch. To be truly virtuous, you have to think good thoughts, speak good words, and do good deeds. That's what Zoroastrianism is about. When these two spirits came together at the beginning, they created life and not life.

At the last judgment, the worst existence will be for followers of the lie, but the best existence to him that follows right. Of these two twin spirits, he who followed the life chose the worst things; the holiest spirit chose right, clothe himself with a massive heavens as a garment.
